whyTempting: The paper ends with a numerical conversion and names a material, radium salts.

whatIsTrue.r0: The paper reports no measurement. It says only that a test with radium salts is not ruled out.
whatIsTrue.r1: The paper's second-to-last sentence is conditional. It is not ruled out ('Es ist nicht ausgeschlossen'), it says, that bodies whose energy content varies to a high degree, such as radium salts, will allow a test of the theory. No experiment is reported, and none is claimed. ME-03's radium card shows how small the effect is: one alpha decay of radium-226 releases 4.871 MeV, which carries off 5.229 mg of mass for every mole that decays.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) The sentence on p. 641 begins 'Es ist nicht ausgeschlossen': it is not ruled out. (2) Its subject: bodies whose energy content can change greatly, with radium salts as the example. (3) Its claim: a test of the theory may succeed with them. (4) What it does not contain: a measured mass, an apparatus or a result. (5) Why radium: its decays release far more energy per gram than any chemical change, yet 5.229 mg per mole, out of the 226 g of a mole of radium-226, is still only about 2.3 parts in 100 000.
whatIsTrue.r3: Quantitative checks of the relation came decades later, from nuclear physics. The paper's own remark stays a proposal.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 18, 639–641 (1905), plate p. 641
